description: Croatia wrote equal treatment and permit-free work for EU nationals into its 2011 Aliens Act, commencing on accession, and the Commission recorded completed legal alignment in 2012; no extracted item links the two. The extracted items give no data on what happened to EU workers in practice.
problem_addressed: In 2007 Croatia's own account in the screening report was that EU migrant workers faced in principle the same work permit conditions as third-country nationals, with limited relief for key staff and permits granted outside the annual quota. The Commission found that Croatia had reached a satisfactory level of alignment in the chapter overall (HRV-EU-2007-001-0020), but that important adjustments were needed on access to the labour market, mainly on non-discrimination against EU migrant workers (HRV-EU-2007-001-0013), including that EU citizens should need no work permit and should not face nationality discrimination in access to employment. The permit elements also belong to RI-FMW-002 and are relied on here because they were the starting point of the reform.
reform_or_mechanism: The Aliens Act in Official Gazette NN 130/2011, passed on 28 October 2011, gives EEA nationals with a right of residence equal rights with Croatian nationals and lets them work without a stay and work permit (Article 153). Article 78(5) relieves EU nationals of the conditions of that article before accession, and Article 236 lets the Government keep earlier rules for nationals of Member States that restrict Croatian workers. Earlier planned amendments to the Act on Foreigners and to the Act on Employment Mediation are recorded in 2007, but their adoption is not stated.
how_implemented: The Act took effect in two steps: it entered into force on 1 January 2012, but Articles 153 to 203 enter into force only on accession, and the Article 78(5) relief ceases on accession. The only applied step after accession in the evidence on the general labour market is a Commission statement in 2015 that Croatia requires a work permit from nationals of restricting Member States (an RI-FMW-002 element). In the public sector, NN 155/2023 provides from 1 January 2024 that EEA and Swiss nationals who know Croatian and the Latin script may be admitted to the civil service (HRV-GOV-2023-001-0004; HRV-GOV-2023-001-0006; an RI-FMW-003 element). No extracted item shows the EU workers chapter being used.
evidence_of_results: No data on EU workers' take-up or experience in the Croatian labour market generally: the extracted items from all eight Croatian sources were searched, not the full source text, and none gives it. The post-accession material is legal in kind: the 2015 permit statement (HRV-EU-2015-001-0004), and a 2023 government bill reporting that the Ombudswoman had pointed to the inconsistency of the Civil Servants Act citizenship condition with EU free movement law and saying that the legislation is being aligned for that reason (HRV-GOV-2023-002-0003; HRV-GOV-2023-002-0004). The Commission's ratings are legal assessments made before accession, not results: Croatia largely fulfilled the requirements on access to the labour market in 2011 (HRV-EU-2011-001-0001), before NN 130/2011 was passed, and had completed alignment in 2012 (HRV-EU-2012-001-0001). A 2023 government text treating a citizenship condition as misaligned sits uneasily with the 2012 completed alignment rating; its scope is the public sector (RI-FMW-003), so this is reported for the analyst and not resolved here.
limitations_of_evidence: The evidence dates from 2007 to 2015 under logged exception LIM-0027, apart from 2023 civil service texts that belong to RI-FMW-003 and are used only for the post-accession statements above. The Commission never says which law closed the gap. Its 2011 report is dated 12 October 2011, while NN 130/2011 was passed on 28 October 2011, published on 16 November 2011 and is a new Act repealing NN 79/07 and 36/09 (HRV-GOV-2011-001-0007), so the amendments the report describes as adopted (HRV-EU-2011-001-0003, under Chapter 23, with no year or Gazette reference) are an earlier unidentified text. The Act is machine translated and capped at Medium. An unofficial English text marked OG 74/13 exists, but only its free excerpt of Articles 1 to 4 was read (HRV-GOV-2013-001-0001) and the rest is on sale, so this use is outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b. The 2023 bill's explanatory statement is machine translated and capped at Medium, reports the Ombudswoman second-hand, and is not a legal text, so it too is outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b. Later amendments to the Aliens Act were not checked. Items in the unmatched queue on Croatian workers moving to other Member States are not used (G5b); one of them, HRV-EU-2015-001-0002, states a treaty end date of 30 June 2020 and is listed for the analyst at G6b. No Croatian item addresses private sector posts reserved for nationals. Filing note: HRV-EU-2012-001-0001 in implementation_items is an EU rating kept as context, not implementation.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's stated position is a foreigners law that makes no distinction for EU citizens, with a requirement that runs to the time of accession and further amendments of unknown content. If it chose to, North Macedonia could use a general foreigners law to carry a separate regime for EU nationals, adopted before accession, as Croatia did. Whether commencing that regime on accession would be enough is untested: the case does not show that this design earned the Commission's rating or that EU workers then had equal access, and it says nothing on reserved private sector posts.
transferable: Two elements need separating. Equal treatment and work without a permit for EU nationals are what the Commission states the acquis requires (HRV-EU-2007-001-0015; MKD-EU-2025-003-0033); this answers the same mechanism as North Macedonia's gap (MEC-01), and North Macedonia's law is within government control and was amended in 2021 and 2025. Cross-case point: commencement on accession is an untested design choice. Croatia's rating is unattributed (HRV-EU-2012-001-0001), Montenegro's deferred clauses cannot yet have been applied (MNE-GOV-2026-001-0005), and Serbia's reported clause (SRB-EU-2015-001-0002) coexisted with Commission findings of misalignment in 2015 and partial alignment in 2024 and 2025 (SRB-EU-2015-001-0010; SRB-EU-2024-001-0004; SRB-EU-2025-001-0005).
not_transferable: Croatia's Act was passed with its accession treaty in view and the source ties it to that treaty, while North Macedonia is at an earlier stage, with its screening report dated 2025. The EU worker provisions read here sit in one Aliens Act and whether other laws were also changed is not known, while North Macedonia has a separate law on employment of foreigners. Reciprocity against restricting Member States depended on Croatia's Act of Accession, and no such terms exist for North Macedonia in the evidence. The evidence gives no measure of size or of EU worker numbers with which to compare the two countries.
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-FMW-001.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Montenegro adopted a separate regime for EU nationals in its foreigners law in December 2025, with named clauses applying only from accession, and Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026; no extracted item links the two. What closed the benchmark is not public, and there are no measured results yet, only an uncorroborated Government claim of improved procedures.
problem_addressed: The Commission recorded no legislative developments on access to the labour market in its 2024 and 2025 reports and recommended finalising legislative alignment. In 2025 it reported early preparations for amendments that would revoke work and other restrictions for EU citizens. These items do not describe the restrictions in detail.
reform_or_mechanism: The Law on amendments to the Law on Foreigners, adopted on 31 December 2025, places the rules on EU nationals in a separate regime (Articles 150 to 178b). New Article 178a gives EU nationals the right to employment under the same conditions as Montenegrin nationals, and Article 152 gives a right to reside for work. Article 78(1)(7v) carves EU nationals out, which a law firm note reads as the annual quota exemption (an RI-FMW-002 element; the unamended Article 78 was not read).
how_implemented: Under new Article 221b the quota exemption and the other listed articles apply only from accession, so those clauses cannot have been applied yet. Article 221b does not list Articles 150 to 178b, but the amending law does not say when Article 178a applies, and the base law's commencement clauses were not read. Secondary acts are due within 12 months of entry into force, and none is in the evidence. The Government's annex states that implementation of the law continued in the reporting period (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0013), which is an uncorroborated self-report naming no clause. The EU release reports that Chapter 2 was provisionally closed, without giving a date or a reason; the date of 15 June 2026 comes only from the Government's annex, which also says this confirmed fulfilment of the closing benchmark. The Government reports 638 residence and work permits to EU citizens from April to August 2026 (an RI-FMW-002 item), and the count does not name the law.
evidence_of_results: No measured outcome found. The extracted items from all twelve Montenegrin sources were searched for data or findings on EU workers' access or treatment under the new law, and none gives any; the full text of the government annex was not read beyond its Chapter 2 section and keyword hits, apart from page 86, which the G6b quality check found. The only stated effect is the Government's claim that applying the new legal solutions further improved procedures, including the exercise of the rights of EU nationals and their family members (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0014). It is one-sided, has no measure and is no proof of success. The clauses deferred to accession cannot yet have results, and for the other clauses the timing is unknown. Provisional closure is a negotiating step and the permit count is a government figure, so neither is an outcome.
limitations_of_evidence: What closed the benchmark is known only from public statements (LIM-0028): the EU common position was not used, the EU release does not say why the chapter closed, and the Government's statement does not say what the benchmark required. No extracted item links the law to the closure, and no Commission assessment of the law is in the evidence. The law is machine translated and capped at Medium, the base law was not read, and the law firm note omits the accession clause. The government annex is also machine translated and capped at Medium. It is proposal text and a self-report, and it conflicts with itself on the venue of the conference (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0001 says Luxembourg; MNE-GOV-2026-003-0004 says Brussels). The closing benchmark statement, the 638 count, MNE-GOV-2026-003-0013 and MNE-GOV-2026-003-0014 rest on it; it is not a legal text, so this use is outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b. The annex cites the Law on Foreigners as also amended by SL 33/2026 (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0015); that text was not read and may bear on the EU regime or Article 221b. It also reports a Blue Card bill under access to the labour market (page 139, not extracted), treated as context. The closure is provisional and the EU may return to the chapter; public posts are RI-FMW-003 and are context only. Filing note: in implementation_items, MNE-EU-2026-002-0001, MNE-EU-2026-002-0002, MNE-EU-2026-002-0004 and MNE-GOV-2026-003-0004 are negotiating steps, and MNE-GOV-2026-003-0006 is a use count; all are kept as context, not implementation.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: the Commission says North Macedonia's foreigners law does not distinguish EU citizens from other foreigners (MKD-EU-2025-001-0097) and that it needs to ensure unrestricted access by accession (MKD-EU-2025-003-0033). On quotas its sources conflict: the Commission asks for EU citizens to be excluded (MKD-EU-2025-003-0028), while the country's own account says quotas do not apply to them following a reciprocity agreement (MKD-EU-2025-003-0010), as validated judgement JDG-009552 reports. If North Macedonia chose this route, it could write an equal-treatment clause and a quota carve-out into its foreigners law, as Montenegro did about six months before the chapter closed, with at least the carve-out deferred to accession. The sequence is suggestive only: it does not show that this law met the benchmark, that deferral was accepted, or that anything changed for EU workers.
transferable: Two elements need separating. Equal treatment in the law is what the Commission asks of North Macedonia (MKD-EU-2025-003-0033), and new Article 178a is a clause expressing it, with its timing unknown; a separate regime for EU nationals inside the foreigners law is a drafting option in principle. The quota element is a neighbouring RI-FMW-002 match, contested as set out in the lesson field, and the validated position is that the evidence shows no benchmark under this issue. Cross-case point: commencement on accession is an untested design choice. Croatia's rating is unattributed (HRV-EU-2012-001-0001), Montenegro's deferred clauses cannot yet have been applied (MNE-GOV-2026-001-0005), and Serbia's reported clause (SRB-EU-2015-001-0002) coexisted with Commission findings of misalignment in 2015 and partial alignment in 2024 and 2025 (SRB-EU-2015-001-0010; SRB-EU-2024-001-0004; SRB-EU-2025-001-0005).
not_transferable: Montenegro's closing benchmark and common position set terms that are not public and may not apply to North Macedonia, which is at an earlier negotiating stage. Montenegro uses one Law on Foreigners, while North Macedonia has a separate law on employment of foreigners. Whether Montenegro's deferral would be accepted elsewhere cannot be judged from the evidence. Only rough measures of size exist, namely 2025 permit quotas of 28 988 in Montenegro (MNE-EU-2025-001-0006) and 10 000 in North Macedonia (MKD-EU-2025-001-0098).
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-FMW-001.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Serbia reported in the 2015 screening report that its 2014 law contains a clause giving EU citizens free access on accession, and it later amended the law to simplify permits, but the Commission still says EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals. This is a stalled case, and no extracted item says why.
problem_addressed: In 2015 the Commission found that Serbia had reached a satisfactory level of alignment in the chapter overall (SRB-EU-2015-001-0008), but that important adjustments were needed on access to the labour market, mainly on non-discrimination against EU migrant workers (SRB-EU-2015-001-0009). It said existing legislation in this area was not yet in line with the acquis, and that by accession EU citizens must not need a work permit. In 2024 and 2025 it found the framework partially aligned because EU citizens are covered by the rules for third-country nationals, which is close in substance to its finding on North Macedonia, though in different words. In 2025 it recommended that Serbia start preparing for alignment.
reform_or_mechanism: By Serbia's own account in 2015, the 2014 Law on Employment of Foreigners provides free access for EU citizens and their family members, entering into force on accession. According to one clause of a secondary study, amendments in 2017 and 2018 were made in order to simplify permit procedures. The Commission says the July 2023 amendments simplified the working permit procedure; the 2023 act sets out a single permit and a labour market test, and it has no separate rule for EU citizens. The Labour Law also prohibits discrimination on grounds of nationality, by Serbia's account. No reform aimed at EU workers' access is visible in what was read, while the content of the 2017, 2018 and 2019 amendments is largely unread and the same study says laws on foreigners were revised in all four countries it covers to include the posting of EU workers (SRB-RES-2021-001-0004).
how_implemented: The 2023 act applied from 1 February 2024; the Commission said in 2024 that the new system had yet to be fully operational and in 2025 that the procedure had been simplified. The Commission reports work permits issued to EU citizens in both years, 2 071 in 2023 and 526 in 2024, so they remain within the permit regime (RI-FMW-002 items); the counts do not name the law they were issued under. No extracted item says whether the deferred free-access clause still stands, and the consolidated law was blocked.
evidence_of_results: No outcome evidence found on access or treatment for EU workers. The extracted items from all eight Serbian sources were searched, not the full source text, and the only stated effect is the Commission's statement that the permit procedure was simplified, for foreigners generally and with no processing data, which is treated here as implementation. The permit counts are not outcomes: totals fall from 50 397 to 17 251, the reports do not explain why, and no extracted item links them to a reform.
limitations_of_evidence: What stalled is clear from the Commission's wording, but no extracted item says why alignment on EU workers has not moved. The 2015 report relays Serbia's account and describes the 2014 law, and the consolidated text (SRB-GOV-2023-003) is inaccessible, so only the 2023 amending act was read, machine translated and capped at Medium. The content of 113/17 and 50/18 is known from one clause of a secondary study, and the 31/19 amendment listed in the register was not read. The amending act's silence on EU citizens does not show that the base law is silent. No Serbian item addresses private sector posts reserved for nationals, and citizenship conditions for public posts are context only (RI-FMW-003). Filing note: in implementation_items, SRB-EU-2024-001-0004, SRB-EU-2025-001-0005, SRB-EU-2024-001-0002 and SRB-EU-2025-001-0002 are EU assessments, and SRB-EU-2024-001-0005 and SRB-EU-2025-001-0006 are use counts; all are kept as context, not implementation.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia is a stalled case with a closely similar Commission finding in different words, covering the permit regime but not reserved private sector posts. It suggests that if North Macedonia amended its foreigners law only to simplify permits for all foreigners, this could earn a chapter-level finding of limited progress while the gap the Commission names remains: permit simplification was one of two stated grounds in each year, with EURES preparations in 2024 and electronic data exchange in 2025. Serbia also reported a general ban on nationality discrimination in the same report that found misalignment, as North Macedonia does now in its own account. It cannot show why the gap persisted or whether a clause deferred to accession is enough.
transferable: The negative point is transferable, conditionally: simplifying permit procedures does not by itself address the difference in treatment that the Commission names, because EU citizens stay inside the foreigner regime. This holds only as far as the Commission's wording supports it, since no extracted item states it as a lesson. Cross-case point: commencement on accession is an untested design choice. Croatia's rating is unattributed (HRV-EU-2012-001-0001), Montenegro's deferred clauses cannot yet have been applied (MNE-GOV-2026-001-0005), and Serbia's reported clause (SRB-EU-2015-001-0002) coexisted with Commission findings of misalignment in 2015 and partial alignment in 2024 and 2025 (SRB-EU-2015-001-0010; SRB-EU-2024-001-0004; SRB-EU-2025-001-0005).
not_transferable: Serbia's negotiating position and the reasons for its slow pace are not in the evidence on this issue, so they cannot be compared with North Macedonia's. The permit reforms read here concern foreigners generally, so they say little about how to draft rules for EU workers. Serbia's 2015 screening is a decade older than North Macedonia's 2025 screening. Only rough measures of size exist, namely EU shares of permits in different years: 3% in Serbia in 2024 (SRB-EU-2025-001-0006) and, by North Macedonia's own account, 12.8% in 2020 and 10.7% in 2021 (MKD-EU-2025-003-0012).
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-FMW-001.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Moldova put a legal duty and sanctions behind MConnect from January 2021, and the operator reports high volumes, but no evidence shows that the sanctions were applied or what changed use. A Court of Accounts page on MConnect was blocked and never read, and is a recorded gap.
problem_addressed: In July 2020 the e-Governance Agency named resistance from data owners, inconsistent data and incompatible systems as obstacles to data exchange. The Court of Accounts, restating its audit of public sector information systems adopted in December 2020, says a large part of those systems do not exchange information (MDA-GOV-2024-001-0005) and that misalignment with government platforms, including MConnect, caused interoperability difficulties (MDA-GOV-2024-001-0004); this predates the 2021 amendments, so it describes the problem and not their implementation. A full-text search of the Commission 2024 and 2025 reports finds no mention of MConnect. The 2025 sentence asking for stronger interoperability between verification systems and state registries concerns asset declarations under Chapter 23 and is flagged theme_doubtful (MDA-EU-2025-001-0001). A 2024 sentence on 14 fragmented systems in the labour ministry (MDA-EU-2024-001-0009) bears on this point but is in the unmatched queue, so it stays unused and is listed for the analyst.
reform_or_mechanism: MConnect was piloted from 2014 to 2018, and Interoperable Europe says Law 142/2018 defines how data exchange happens through it. Amendments effective on 18 January 2021 wrote into Article 6 of that law the duty not to ask for documents available through the platform, and added fines and temporary disqualification from a post to the Code of Contraventions. The operator also states a free data rule between public participants, a duty on participants to make their data sets available, and, in 2020 slides, an access route intended for participants with no information system, with no later confirmation that it operates.
how_implemented: The operator reports 480+ public and private institutions connected, 2.6+ million requests a day and 600 million exchanges in total, under 2024 figures on its own page. The only independent evidence is the Court of Accounts follow-up of September 2024, which concerns public sector information systems and not MConnect as such. It reports that connecting one named system was still under analysis, and that it was shown no evidence that a planned exchange between two systems was carried out or works. A full-text search of the Moldovan sources held finds no statement that any fine or disqualification has been applied.
evidence_of_results: No outcome evidence on the 2021 amendments or on use by institutions found. Searched in full text: the operator's MConnect page, its 2020 slides, 2021 notice and 2025 project summary, the 2026 state news report, the agency's 2023 survey summary (MDA-GOV-2024-002), the civil society analysis (MDA-CSO-2023-001), the Commission 2024 and 2025 reports, the 2024 Interoperable Europe supporting document and the Court of Accounts follow-up. MDA-CSO-2023-001, MDA-GOV-2024-002 and MDA-GOV-2026-001 do not name MConnect. None measures use by institutions over time, documents no longer requested, or any effect of the 2021 amendments. Separately, the Commission says in 2025 that access and use of digital public services significantly increased (MDA-EU-2025-001-0009), with no figure and no named platform; this is on the citizen side and is not linked to the amendments.
limitations_of_evidence: Every use figure is the operator's own, is machine translated and capped at Medium, combines public and private bodies and has no earlier figure to compare with. The two volume figures do not reconcile: 2.6 million a day would pass 600 million in about 230 days, so they may count different things. A Court of Accounts page whose URL refers to an examination of MConnect (MDA-GOV-2021-001; title from the URL, page not read) returned HTTP 403 and the MConnect statistics dataset returned 404, so neither is evidence here, and the wording seen only in search excerpts at country selection is not used (LIM-0028). The operator's page and the Court of Accounts follow-up are machine translated, capped at Medium and not legal texts, so their use is outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b. Interoperable Europe's general remark that Moldova is on the right track (MDA-IO-2024-002-0005) is not evidence of implementation and is not relied on. Claims of absence in this case rest on a full-text search of the eleven Moldovan source texts held for MConnect, interoperability and the sanctions, and on the extracted items classified to this issue.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia already has a legal obligation to use its platform (MKD-GOV-2022-004-0050), and its 2023 strategy says competence to inspect laws on ICT use is not established (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0029), so Moldova's sanctions may be the closest parallel in these cases. The evidence stops at the text of the law: it does not show that the sanctions were applied or that they raised use. If North Macedonia considered a sanction in law, this case could show only that such a mechanism exists on paper and is untested here, and that a connection count, such as 480+, may not show regular use.
transferable: The wording of a duty on officials and bodies backed by a personal sanction could be copied into comparable administrative law, but the case gives no evidence that it would raise use, and no item states a lesson. The access route stated in 2020 for participants with no information system speaks to a related barrier, North Macedonia's lack of communications software (MKD-EU-2023-001-0153), but the only source is a 2020 slide with no later confirmation.
not_transferable: Moldova's connection count includes private bodies and has no activity threshold, so it cannot be set against North Macedonia's 58 connected and 33 active institutions (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0064). North Macedonia's stated barriers are IT staff, software, coordination and process change (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0065), which a sanction does not itself supply. In the full text of its 2024 and 2025 reports, the Commission does not name MConnect, whereas in North Macedonia data exchange sits in a Reform Agenda payment condition (MKD-EU-2024-007-0016).
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-028.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Serbia has a 2016 legal duty to exchange data and a Bus to which the Commission says more databases are connected, but no source measures use by institutions. Around half of surveyed citizens still report being asked for documents the state holds.
problem_addressed: The Ministry describes citizens acting as couriers between administrations, collecting certificates from several counters. WeBER reports that the once-only principle is not applied consistently, with around 53 to 54% of surveyed citizens saying they had to submit documents the state already held the last time they requested a service. Two Commission sentences, on fragmented responsibilities and on aligning sector law with the procedure law (SRB-EU-2025-001-0008, SRB-EU-2025-001-0011), bear on this point but are in the unmatched queue, so they stay unused and are listed for the analyst.
reform_or_mechanism: The Law on General Administrative Procedure of 2016 obliges administrations to exchange data and documents from official records among themselves, and introduced the once-only principle. The e-ZUP system was established in June 2017 on the basis of that law and is now the Government Service Bus. An improved Bus was launched in December 2023, and the Commission says an interoperability framework is in place.
how_implemented: The Commission states in 2024 and 2025 that more databases are connected to the Bus, with no number and no volume of use. The Ministry reports more than 170 million data exchanged in six years, and on an undated page 18 databases of eight institutions. WeBER says its research confirmed the once-only principle is implemented in a sample of seven services, except property registration, where it is unclear whether it is or can be applied. The report says points come from observing seven sample services, but it does not say what was observed for its 3/3 score, and it does not name the Bus or eZUP.
evidence_of_results: The Ministry claims nearly 500,000 citizen hours and about RSD 20 million saved in the first year, and describes eEnrolment as removing paper documents, with no method given. WeBER's February 2025 survey (N = 1006) found around 53 to 54% had to submit documents already held by the state at their last request, while 68% agreed in general terms that they are not required to, and WeBER scores citizen experience 0.5/2. No source text searched gives use of the Bus by institution over time. As a proxy for data reuse, the Regional Cooperation Council scores Serbia's pre-filled forms at 61 in 2023 and 62 in 2025, against a regional average of 65 and an EU average of 71, and says this indicates potential to enhance data reuse (ALB-IO-2026-001-0042, ALB-IO-2026-001-0043, ALB-IO-2026-001-0044). The index does not name the Bus, and no cause is inferred.
limitations_of_evidence: The savings are a Ministry self-report with no comparison group, and they describe a period before the run's window (flagged out_of_window). The survey measures citizen perception at one date, is not linked to any database or service, and sits against the 3/3 score on sampled services. That score is an implementation indicator with no basis stated in this report; on the same indicator the Montenegrin report gives points because document lists are published (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0026), so it is not shown to rest on observed exchange. The 170 million figure is a volume of exchange and is treated here as implementation, although second-pass classification noted it as outcome. The survey items are listed under results although second-pass classification noted them as implementation, because WeBER itself labels E 1.14 as outcomes and impact. WeBER is EU-funded with the Ministry named as a project associate. The Ministry's 2023 statement that buying real estate is now done automatically (SRB-GOV-2023-002-0006) may conflict with WeBER on property registration (SRB-CSO-2025-001-0010), or they may concern different steps; this is not settled. The pre-filled forms score is from a source rated partly independent; the 2025 value comes from desk research, so the method may differ from 2023. The same index scores North Macedonia at 73 and 75 (ALB-IO-2026-001-0045), so it may not track use of an exchange platform. Claims of absence in this case rest on a full-text search of the eight Serbian source texts held for the Bus, e-ZUP and the system's other name, and on the extracted items classified to this issue.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia does not show what raises institutional use, because no source text searched measures it. It suggests that a legal duty and a live exchange system, with more databases connected, may sit alongside about half of surveyed citizens reporting they were still asked for documents. If so, this would be relevant to North Macedonia's conflict between telling the screening that once-only is applied and its Reform Agenda saying institutions do not gather evidence ex officio (MKD-EU-2023-003-0029, MKD-GOV-2024-001-0097). The lesson goes no further than this: connection and a review of sampled services may not settle whether evidence is obtained ex officio.
transferable: The mechanism of a procedural duty to exchange data, with a central system built on it, matches North Macedonia's own Law on General Administrative Procedure and platform. WeBER's measures, a citizen survey on documents resubmitted alongside a review of sampled services, could be applied wherever the same monitor runs; the Serbian and Montenegrin reports share the indicators.
not_transferable: North Macedonia's stated problem is institutions not using the platform, while Serbia's evidence is on the citizen side and does not name the platform. The undated 18 databases of eight institutions cannot be set against North Macedonia's 58 connected and 33 active institutions, because they count different things. No source read connects Serbia's position to its accession stage or to an EU payment condition on data exchange, so that difference is not tested.
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-028.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Montenegro's register pairs in active exchange are reported as 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on government figures with no stated cause. The Commission still finds register integration and once-only incomplete, and an official says strengthening the inspection was not achieved because of staffing delays.
problem_addressed: The Commission says in 2024 and 2025 that the Law on Administrative Procedure is not consistently implemented, notably on once-only and electronic communication. In 2025 it adds that integrating all public registers into the exchange system is incomplete; in 2024 it recommended working towards interoperability of registers through the Reform Agenda. The Ministry names insufficient data available through web services and slow settling of legal and organisational preconditions as the obstacles to full interoperability. Its official also says some public bodies are not meeting their obligations under the Law on Electronic Administration, and citizens contact institutions one by one.
reform_or_mechanism: The Ministry of Public Administration established JSERP, a single system for electronic data exchange between state bodies, and a Metaregister. A new X-Road platform has since been established, according to a government text of 2026. The Law on Electronic Government, the once-only principle and the Reform Agenda sit around it, and expanding JSERP to connect all registers is proposed in the 2026 to 2029 open government plan.
how_implemented: Government reporting gives 21 institutions with access in both the 2024 report and the 2026 text, which is marked as a proposal, while active register pairs are reported as 18 and then 37, and 8 million queries in 2024. The share of catalogue e-services that can draw on more than one register in one query was 0 in 2023 and 2024, against a target of 10% by 2024 (MNE-GOV-2025-002-0015). The Commission reports some progress on data exchange in 2024 and incomplete register integration in 2025. Strengthening the information society inspection was not achieved, which an official puts down to delays in the staffing plan.
evidence_of_results: The Ministry claims that JSERP has significantly improved electronic service delivery, with no figure. The Institute Alternative survey of February 2025 (1010 citizens) found 53.6% aware they need not provide documents the state holds and 19.9% reporting once-only in practice, and scores citizen experience 0/2. These concern the once-only principle, and no source text searched links them to JSERP. As a proxy for data reuse, the Regional Cooperation Council scores Montenegro's pre-filled forms at 24 in 2023 and 49 in 2025, against a regional average of 65 and an EU average of 71, and describes this as weaker than the regional average (ALB-IO-2026-001-0025, ALB-IO-2026-001-0031, ALB-IO-2026-001-0044). The index does not name JSERP, and no cause is inferred.
limitations_of_evidence: All direct figures on platform use are government self-reports, machine translated and capped at Medium; the implementation report and the second contribution to the Commission report are not legal texts, so their use is outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b. The 2026 text is marked as a proposal (PREDLOG), and an unchanged 21 alongside the Metaregister jump may be a figure carried forward. The only indicator of data reuse from outside national government is the pre-filled forms score, from a source rated partly independent: it is not a measure of platform use, the 2025 value comes from desk research so the method may differ from 2023, and the same index scores North Macedonia at 73 and 75 (ALB-IO-2026-001-0045), so it may not track use of an exchange platform. The base of the 19.9% is unclear, and the 3/3 score for practice rests on published lists of documents, not on observed exchange (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0026). The survey items are listed under results although second-pass classification noted them as implementation, because the source labels E 1.14 as outcomes and impact. Institute Alternative's report names the Ministry, which established JSERP, as a project associate, and its event report names the Ministry as a co-funder. The Metaregister figures of 45, 170+ and 265 may count different things and are not a trend. The SIGMA finding on special laws reaches us second-hand, since SIGMA 2024 was blocked (LIM-0028). A major cybersecurity crisis delayed digital services, which further clouds any before and after reading; sources conflict on its date, 2023 in the Commission's 2025 report (MNE-EU-2025-001-0010) and 2022 in its 2024 report (MNE-EU-2024-001-0014) and the open government plan (MNE-GOV-2025-001-0004). Claims of absence in this case rest on a full-text search of the Montenegrin source texts held for JSERP, X-Road, the Metaregister and electronic data exchange, and on the extracted items classified to this issue.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro gives two reported points on use, not a series: active register pairs of 18 and then 37 while institutions with access stay at 21, on unverified government figures, the later from a proposal text. No source text searched says why, although a new X-Road platform is reported in between. Its stated obstacles, data not available through web services and slow settling of legal and organisational preconditions, resemble North Macedonia's need to digitalise registers, change processes and integrate software (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0065). An official reports that strengthening the inspection was not achieved, and no extracted item shows whether it has acted on data exchange, so the case says nothing on inspection as a lever. If the figures hold, the case suggests that counts of connected institutions and of active exchanges may move separately.
transferable: The underlying mechanism, a central exchange system with a catalogue of registers and a count of active pairs, is close to North Macedonia's platform and could be measured the same way. The stated preconditions, data available through web services and settled legal and organisational arrangements, are institutional rather than specific to Montenegro.
not_transferable: Montenegro's 21 institutions have access to a platform reported as under development in the April 2025 report and as established in the September 2026 text, whereas North Macedonia's audit refers to connecting around 1,300 institutions (MKD-GOV-2022-004-0051) and its platform has been in place since 2015 (MKD-EU-2023-003-0040), so scale and starting point differ. The active register pair is not the same measure as North Macedonia's active institution (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0186). Both countries have a Reform Agenda, but Montenegro's is cited only in a Commission recommendation, and no source says how it affected use.
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-028.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Moldova digitalised services through a long donor-backed project and assisted access, and reports online use rising, with service-level data for 2022 showing most digital services unused. The rise rests on agency and funder reporting, and no extracted item shows what caused it.
problem_addressed: Moldova counted many services as digital while few were fully digital and many were unused: a 2023 brief found 36 of 157 services that could be requested online were provided in digital format, and 128 of the 226 services reported as digital had no users in 2022. The Commission still named low demand, especially in rural areas, as limiting use of e-government services in its 2025 report.
reform_or_mechanism: The main measures are the World Bank-financed Modernization of Government Services project run by the e-Governance Agency, the Public Services Portal, the EVO app launched in June 2024, assisted access through Unified Public Service Centres (CUPS), and a strategy approved in September 2023 with digitalisation targets. The approach is service-by-service digitalisation with assisted access. No extracted item records a legal duty on institutions or users to use one portal.
how_implemented: Offered: the Commission reports 15 online services launched on the electronic services platform in its 2024 report and two in 2025, and over 50% of mapped services available 'fully or partially'. Fully transactional: the only figure with a stated definition is the 2023 brief's 36 of 157, because the agency's 283 e-services include partly automated ones and its 303 of 648 'fully digitalized' (2025) and 445 of 636 'accessed digitally' (2026) are unverified. EVO lists all services 'regardless of how they are provided', so a listing there is not a transaction. The Commission confirms 105 CUPS, but no extracted item says how many people they served.
evidence_of_results: Used: the 2022 service-level data show 128 of 226 digital services with no users, 77 of them with requests at counters and 51 with no requests on any channel, and this count has not been repeated. The agency's survey reports online access passing offline access (54.5% against 52.6%), and the agency reports 71% of 4.5 million requests submitted online in January to June 2026, up 7 points on 2025. The Commission states that access and use 'significantly increased', with no figure and no named cause. No extracted item measures use of the Public Services Portal or EVO themselves.
limitations_of_evidence: Figures on online requests and access after 2023 come from the agency, a survey it commissioned or the project's funder, or have no stated source (the observatory's 'only 20% of requests' at counters for businesses in June 2024, MDA-IO-2024-002-0008), and no independent check on portal use was found in the extracted items; the request series does not say which services it counts. The Commission's e-signature user figures measure signature use only; they sit in the unmatched queue (MDA-EU-2024-001-0006, MDA-EU-2025-001-0006), stay unused under G5b and are listed for the analyst. The rise from 25% to over 54% of citizens has no stated base, and a similar 2023 survey figure is reported for people who used public services, not all citizens. Blocked sources, including the SIGMA 2024 reports, are a recorded gap (LIM-0028). Use figures are listed as outcome items here although pass 2 classed them as implementation, because use is the result this issue asks about. The Court of Accounts report relied on in the INT-MDA-0019 and INT-MDA-0022 rows (MDA-GOV-2024-001-0004) is machine translated, capped at Medium and flagged possible_misread; it is an audit report and not a legal text, so it is outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b. Claims of absence in this case refer to the extracted items, not the full source text.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's stated mechanism includes low uptake of a working portal (MEC-11), and the Commission's 2024 report gives 292,179 users and 2,070 monthly applications, with no reference period beyond 'currently' (MKD-EU-2024-001-0024). If North Macedonia's position resembles Moldova's, a count of digital services would say little about use, since more than half of those reported for 2022 had no users, although 51 of the 128 had no demand on any channel. Moldova also reports use rising alongside service redesign and assisted access, but it does not show which measure raised it, so any of them would be a hypothesis to test.
transferable: A one-off count, made service by service and separating fully from partly digital services, showed the gap in Moldova in 2022, and it could help with North Macedonia's conflicting service counts if repeated. Moldova has not repeated it and still reports differing counts (283, 303 of 648, 445 of 636), so it has not shown that such a count settles a conflict. Assisted access answers a barrier for which North Macedonia so far plans only an analysis for establishing DigInfo centres or upgrading one-stop-shop centres (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0127, machine translated), and its effect on use in Moldova is unmeasured, so it transfers only as an idea to test.
not_transferable: The Moldovan results sit within a seven-year donor project and a dedicated agency, while North Macedonia's ownership is described as fragmented, with 101 of 242 foreseen posts unfilled (MKD-EU-2023-003-0045; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0076). The observatory factsheet describes EVO as a modular app with the Public Service Portal as one module and the business portal as an extension of MCabinet, and the agency calls EVO the single government portal and plans to centralise all access under it (MDA-IO-2024-002-0014; MDA-IO-2024-002-0012; MDA-IO-2024-002-0002; MDA-GOV-2026-001-0005; MDA-GOV-2025-001-0018). That single-portal claim is recent and unverified, and no extracted item measures use of EVO or the portal, so Moldova offers no tested single-portal model. North Macedonia's increase in e-services is a Reform Agenda condition (MKD-EU-2024-007-0015), and no extracted item shows the same condition for Moldova; relative size was not assessed because no extracted item gives it.
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-036.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Albania placed most services on e-Albania, with a 2023 law obliging institutions to use it, and an international source reports high use. Full transactions are not established, payment often fails, and no extracted item shows that the law or the portal caused the reported use.
problem_addressed: Albania's gap is reported mainly as depth and inclusion: the Commission records 95% of applications for 1,237 services offered online in 2024 and 1,253 in 2025, yet accessibility for vulnerable groups remains unaddressed. The sources conflict on range, because the RCC also says Albania 'continues to lag behind the regional average in certain aspects of service scope and sophistication', with a citizen services score of 50 against 53 from desk research in 2025. It also asks Albania to improve access to the use of e-services and to address an emerging digital divide. The national monitor finds digitalisation largely complete but citizens not at the centre of design and delivery.
reform_or_mechanism: Law No. 43/2023 on Electronic Governance, adopted in June 2023, requires public institutions to use e-Albania as the primary point of access and requires e-payment through the portal; as stated in the sources, the duty falls on institutions, not users. The Digital Agenda 2022-2026 sets a 95% target. ADISA was absorbed by the National Agency for Information Society, which concentrates policy and operational control.
how_implemented: Offered: the monitor records more than 90% of services placed on the portal since its previous cycle and most physical counters closed, while municipal offices still handle services that need in-person steps. Fully transactional: no extracted item gives a national count, and of seven sampled services the monitor calls two end-to-end, while its own footnote says the payment option usually does not work, and others, such as vehicle registration and VAT, need in-person payment. No service is yet delivered as a life event. Vehicle registration and VAT are described as offered outside the portal in one passage and as sampled services needing in-person payment in another.
evidence_of_results: Used: the Regional Cooperation Council (RCC) reports e-government users at 78.5% of internet users in 2023 and 88.6% in 2024, with 3.43 million registered users and 15.2 million services provided in 2024 and 17 million in 2025. The monitor's perception survey has 66.9% agreeing that they can access services easily online and 30.5% disagreeing. No extracted item gives the share of those services that were completed online from start to finish.
limitations_of_evidence: The RCC gives no origin for the portal figures and does not define a registered user or a service provided; its text says 89% of the population where its table says 88.6% of internet users. The e-government user indicator counts any online contact with authorities, not portal use (ALB-IO-2026-001-0046). The extracted items hold no series from before the June 2023 law, so use before and after it cannot be compared. The monitor's informant scores are points awarded only if all informants agree (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0078; 0 of 3 on accessible service delivery, 3 of 3 on ease of use), so they are not counts of people. The monitor states that 'these reforms explain why' informants describe transactional reliability and ease of access (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0006), but this rests on three informants, concerns their views and not use, and conflicts with its footnote that payment 'usually does not work' (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0043). The monitor also reports the law's once-only duty both ways, as effectively implemented (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0017) and as partial (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0010, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0057, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0059, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0065); these items sit in the unmatched queue, stay unused under G5b and are listed for the analyst. Claims of absence in this case refer to the extracted items, not the full source text.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia's 2025 strategy proposes updating the law towards mandatory integration or connection of each e-service on the portal (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0194, machine translated), and its stated mechanisms include coordination failure (MEC-08) and low uptake (MEC-11). Albania shows that a duty on institutions can sit alongside most services being placed on one portal and high reported use, but no extracted item shows that the duty caused either, and the legal e-payment duty is reported as limited in practice. If North Macedonia adopted such a duty, this case would not support expecting it to drive use; it supports, at most, the RCC's untested statement that uptake is linked to the portal's central role.
transferable: The monitor reports that absorbing ADISA into the agency removed one named overlap, on monitoring, evaluation and reporting between ADISA and the Agency for Dialogue and Co-governance (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0080; ALB-CSO-2025-001-0076). This is a narrow result with no measure, and North Macedonia already has a lead ministry that lacks resources and cooperation (MKD-EU-2023-003-0045), so naming one body would not by itself address its problem. A legal duty on institutions to integrate services is an untested option: no extracted item shows that it caused Albania's range, and Albania's experience shows that working payment and signature cannot be assumed.
not_transferable: Closing counters cannot be assumed to transfer: the source gives no count, date or effect on users, and North Macedonia has 1,120 services available only in person and an audit finding that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0055; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0136, both machine translated). Albania's own unaddressed accessibility issues show that its route has not solved this. Relative size was not assessed because no extracted item gives it. In these items the Commission's ask of Albania is a recommendation, while North Macedonia's increase in e-services is also a Reform Agenda condition (MKD-EU-2024-007-0015).
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-036.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Montenegro launched a new portal in December 2024 and a plan for transactional services, but sampled core services were not on it and use on the broad indicator fell before it launched. This case is too early and unverified, and its delivery figures rest on the government's own report.
problem_addressed: Montenegro's government names low use of e-services and weak interoperability as key challenges, and the Commission repeatedly asks it to prioritise a platform for transactional services. The national monitor reports that the government's own Digital Services Plan 2025-2027 puts no service at the fifth level (full online service). E-government users were 37.5% of internet users in 2024, below the Western Balkans average of 54%.
reform_or_mechanism: Sources date the new eUprava portal differently in kind: the government adopted an information note on it in December 2024, when the monitor says it 'was not functional'; the Commission and the event report say it launched that month; and first services were published in April 2025. It runs under a plan for transactional services 2025-2027 covering 171 services and 21 institutions, revised on 18 December 2025; the RCC says the same plan sets out 162 additional services and the revised plan's table sums to 175, and these figures are not reconciled. The Law on Electronic Government gives the legal basis, and the government launched an initiative for all institutions to publish their services on the portal. A proposed Open Government action plan targets 150 transactional services by 2029.
how_implemented: Offered: the government reports 106 services from 14 institutions on the portal, without saying how many are transactional, and eFirma and eTaxis run outside it. Fully transactional: the government's action plan states 45 transactional services (MNE-GOV-2025-001-0009), while its Digital Services Plan 2025-2027, as cited by the monitor, puts no service at level 5 (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0012). These are two government statements not shown to be at the same date (the action plan is dated 12 October 2025; the monitor, dated September 2025, does not date the plan's state of play), not reconciled, and no extracted item holds an independent count of transactional services. Delivery against the plan was 25 of 57 by July 2025, then 57 of 57 on the government's own report, with no independent check in the extracted items. The ministry reports two officials in the responsible directorate, a refusal of budget reserve for Interior services and Employment Agency services waiting on a new law. The ministry's report on the Digital Transformation Strategy gives 43.14% of planned 2024 activities fulfilled, for the whole strategy and not only e-services (government reporting, machine translated; repeated by the monitor, MNE-CSO-2025-001-0031).
evidence_of_results: Used: e-government users fell from 48.4% of internet users in 2023 to 37.5% in 2024, on an indicator of any online contact with authorities (ALB-IO-2026-001-0046), and an oral UNDP figure puts actual use at 8%. No extracted item gives use of eUprava itself. The monitor's service delivery grades reflect findings to the end of 2024, when the portal was under construction (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0028; MNE-CSO-2025-001-0027). Its statements that information improved and that none of the seven sampled services was on the portal are notes made at the time of writing, after the first services of April 2025. The government states that satisfaction is around 50%.
limitations_of_evidence: The portal is young. The monitor, a non-government body co-funded by the monitored ministry (SQ-00180), sets its findings to the end of 2024, when the portal was under construction, with later notes to July 2025 (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0028; MNE-CSO-2025-001-0027), so its grades largely predate the first services, and the government's report of full delivery and the 106 count are untested. The RCC text says use continues to grow, against the fall in its own table. The 8% figure is oral, second-hand and has no reference period, and the event report is rated Low. The 2024 user figures predate almost all of the portal's life, so they measure the starting position. The 106 services, 25 and 57 of 57, the 43.14%, the two officials, the budget refusal and 'key challenges' come from machine-translated Montenegrin government reports, capped at Medium; they are not legal texts, so they are outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b, and item MNE-GOV-2025-002-0008 is also flagged possible_misread. Claims of absence in this case refer to the extracted items, not the full source text.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro is the closest parallel to North Macedonia's position of a live portal, the most-needed services absent and capacity gaps (MEC-03, MEC-11; MKD-EU-2024-001-0021), but its results are too early and unverified. It suggests a hypothesis, not a finding: a portal launched without the most-needed services on it may improve information without improving the service, which is the monitor's statement, drawn from seven sampled services, with grades that largely predate the first services. It also suggests that where a plan reports a delivered count, an independent check on whether services are transactional may be needed, given North Macedonia's own conflicting counts.
transferable: As a conditional hypothesis only: a portal may add little where the services people need sit elsewhere, and North Macedonia's Commission findings say the most commonly requested services are not yet online (MKD-EU-2024-001-0021). It rests on one monitor and seven sampled services, whose grades largely predate the first services, that monitor also reports a gain in information, and no extracted item measures use of eUprava. The stated constraints of too few staff and refused budget have a parallel in North Macedonia's unfilled posts and limited resources for the ministry (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0076; MKD-EU-2023-003-0045).
not_transferable: The Montenegrin portal launched in December 2024 on the Commission's account, while North Macedonia's has run since 2019 (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0021) and has a longer record of low use, so results at Montenegro's stage may not predict results at a later one. The cybersecurity crisis that the Commission dates to 2023 and says delayed services and eroded trust (the government's action plan refers instead to 'the 2022 attacks', MNE-GOV-2025-001-0004, classed out_of_scope at pass 2) has no stated equivalent in North Macedonia's evidence here. Montenegro's different accession stage was not used as a reason, because no extracted item links it to the portal.
notes: Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-01/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-036.csv; proposed until G6b Validated at G6b (GATE-0011).

description: Croatia prepared the European Health Insurance Card before its accession on 1 July 2013: a regulation on the card was adopted in December 2011, the Commission found preparations reaching completion in October 2012, and the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) reports issuing the card in 2013 and EU visitors using it. Croatia already had a central health information system (CEZIH), migrated to new hardware in 2012, and by 2013 HZZO was issuing national health insurance cards alongside the EHIC, so the case shows the end state Moldova is working towards rather than how to build the missing preconditions. All statements of results come from HZZO's own reports.
problem_addressed: In October 2011 the Commission reported that preparations continued for the introduction of the card upon accession (HRV-EU-2011-001-0004). No Croatian source in the project describes a missing precondition of the kind Moldova faces: in 2012 the Commission found Croatia advanced in the area of e-health, without linking this to the card (HRV-EU-2012-001-0007), and in 2013 one HZZO service issued national health insurance cards and smart cards alongside the EHIC and managed the public key infrastructure that is the basis for using CEZIH (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0005). A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project for the card, health insurance cards and the health information system found none that states when the national card or CEZIH was introduced.
reform_or_mechanism: The reform is the introduction of the card upon accession (INT-HRV-0012), with a Regulation on the EHIC adopted in December 2011 that set the card's validity (one year for all insured persons, longer if necessary for posted workers and their family members), its form as a separate card and the other details needed to issue it (HRV-EU-2012-001-0006; INT-HRV-0013). The source names neither the issuing body nor the regulation's Croatian title. HZZO also agreed with the foreign and defence ministries a procedure for issuing the card to their officials (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0004; INT-HRV-0017). Work on the information systems ran in parallel: a hardware contract and migration of CEZIH and of HZZO's central information system, to be completed by May 2013 (HRV-GOV-2013-002-0001; INT-HRV-0014; INT-HRV-0015), a tender for consolidating all registers in the health system (HRV-GOV-2013-002-0002; INT-HRV-0016), and further upgrades of both systems planned for 2013 (HRV-GOV-2013-002-0003; HRV-GOV-2013-002-0004). None of these sources links the systems to the card.
how_implemented: In October 2012, nine months before accession, the Commission reported that preparations in relation to the card were reaching completion (HRV-EU-2012-001-0005). In 2013 one HZZO service issued and personalised the card together with national health insurance cards and smart cards (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0005). Two HZZO regional offices give issuing figures for 2013: Rijeka processed 35,124 requests for European cards and 5,320 for certificates (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0002), and Split issued 8,781 cards and certificates together (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0003); the Rijeka text does not spell out that 'European cards' are the EHIC or that 'certificates' are the provisional replacement certificate. Whether the procedure for officials was agreed before or after accession is not stated (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0004).
evidence_of_results: The only statements of results come from HZZO, the body that issues the card. It says it was fully ready for accession thanks to intense preparations (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0001) and began to function without major obstacles in the European bodies for social security coordination (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0007). It says a vast number of EU insured persons received health care during their stay in Croatia by using the card (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0006), and that, although accession at the height of the tourist season was an added challenge, all EU citizens on holiday who needed care received adequate care (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0008; HRV-GOV-2014-001-0009); the last two passages do not name the card. None of these statements is quantified. A search of all 68 Croatian evidence passages in the project, including those from the Commission's 2015 report, found no independent account of the card after accession.
limitations_of_evidence: All Croatian evidence dates from 2011 to 2014, before the period normally covered, and is used by logged exception. The HZZO reports are the issuing body's own accounts; their Croatian passages are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence, while the English foreword and the English passage on EHIC use (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0001; HRV-GOV-2014-001-0006) are not translated. Issuing figures exist for two regional offices only, with no national total, and the Split figure does not separate cards from certificates. The passages on the information systems do not name the card, so their part in it is not shown, and the completion of the 2012 migration and of the planned 2013 upgrades is not reported. HZZO's statement that it adapted all its contracted providers (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0009) is not tied to any recorded intervention.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Croatia shows the end state that Moldova's preparations aim at, with the health insurer issuing both the national card and the EHIC by 2013, working from a central health information system, and a secondary act fixing the card's validity, form and issuing details about 18 months before accession. Moldova's draft CNAM order on the card's technical specifications and the provisional replacement certificate (MDA-GOV-2025-002-0098) is the nearest counterpart of Croatia's 2011 regulation. The case does not show how to build a national card or an integrated health information system where none exists, which is Moldova's gap (MDA-EU-2025-001-0076).
transferable: A secondary act on the card's validity, form and issuing, adopted well before accession (HRV-EU-2012-001-0006); an identified issuing body, as HZZO was in Croatia, which in Moldova would be CNAM, already the coordinator of EHIC implementation (MDA-GOV-2025-002-0068); provision for particular groups such as posted workers and officials (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0004); and preparing contracted providers to treat visitors from Member States, which HZZO's own account presents as its main test at accession (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0008; HRV-GOV-2014-001-0009).
not_transferable: Croatia's starting point: a central health information system already in use and migrated to new hardware in 2012, national health insurance cards issued by HZZO by 2013, and a Commission finding in 2012 that Croatia was advanced in e-health (HRV-GOV-2013-002-0001; HRV-GOV-2014-001-0005; HRV-EU-2012-001-0007), against Moldova's lack of a national card and of an integrated health information system (MDA-EU-2025-001-0076; MDA-EU-2024-001-0071). Croatia prepared for a fixed accession date (HRV-GOV-2014-001-0001). The evidence is 12 to 15 years old, so the technology and costs of a card system then are no guide now.
notes: RUN-2026-02 comparator step (target Moldova). Comparator case for RUN-2026-02 (Moldova), RI-FMW-015. LIM-0049 (out_of_window) and LIM-0050 (machine translation, Medium cap) apply.

description: Montenegro recognises the European Health Insurance Card in its Law on compulsory health insurance but will introduce it only after accession, in wording the Commission repeats in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Asked in 2025 for a feasibility study, it updated one with 2025 data and in February 2026 adopted an action plan for social security coordination that sets out the technical and IT upgrades needed before accession. Chapter 2 was provisionally closed in June 2026, but no source in the project links the closure to the card, the card has not been issued and the Commission still asks for the health information system to be adapted.
problem_addressed: In 2025 the Commission's key recommendation was to prepare a feasibility study on the impact of the card on public finances by the end of 2025 (MNE-EU-2025-001-0019; MNE-EU-2025-001-0022). As the Commission reports it, the updated study found a basic legal and administrative framework in place, with technical and information capacities still to be strengthened (MNE-EU-2026-003-0010). The 2026 key recommendation asks Montenegro to improve its existing Integrated Health Information System and adapt it for issuing and applying the card, to equip the Health Insurance Fund with technical and administrative capacity and resources, and to budget for future reimbursements, all by accession (MNE-EU-2026-003-0005). This is the same mechanism as Moldova's, weak administrative capacity, with a budget element that matches insufficient resources in substance.
reform_or_mechanism: Legal recognition of the card in the Law on compulsory health insurance, with its introduction deferred to accession (MNE-EU-2024-001-0020; MNE-EU-2025-001-0021; MNE-EU-2026-003-0007; INT-MNE-0026); the adoption date of the provision is not stated. A feasibility study on introducing the card (INT-MNE-0027). The Action Plan for the Coordination of Social Security Systems 2026-2028, defining key activities, deadlines and institutional responsibilities (MNE-EU-2026-003-0006; INT-MNE-0028). The existing Integrated Health Information System, which is to be adapted for the card (MNE-EU-2026-003-0005; INT-MNE-0029).
how_implemented: The feasibility study was updated with 2025 statistical data and, as the Commission reports it, confirmed no significant financial obstacles to implementing the card (MNE-EU-2026-003-0008; MNE-EU-2026-003-0009). Its findings were integrated into the action plan, which outlines the technical and IT upgrades required before accession (MNE-EU-2026-003-0011), and the Government adopted the plan in February 2026 (MNE-EU-2026-003-0006). The Commission rated progress in the chapter as good in 2026 and named preparation for the card through the plan among its reasons (MNE-EU-2026-003-0003; MNE-EU-2026-003-0004). A search of all 204 Montenegrin evidence passages in the project for the card, the health information system and the Health Insurance Fund found none reporting any of the plan's EHIC upgrades carried out, and the dates of the original study and its update are not stated.
evidence_of_results: No result yet: the card is to be introduced only after accession (MNE-EU-2026-003-0007). The same search of all 204 Montenegrin evidence passages found none reporting the card issued, the system adapted or the Fund equipped. Chapter 2 was provisionally closed at the Accession Conference (MNE-EU-2026-002-0001), on 15 June 2026 according to the Government (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0002), which says the closure confirmed fulfilment of the closing benchmark (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0004). Neither source names the card, and the Commission's 2026 key recommendation, issued after the closure, still asks for the card's preconditions by accession, so the closure is a negotiating step and not a result on this issue.
limitations_of_evidence: Everything on the card comes from the Commission's reports: the feasibility study and the action plan themselves are not among the sources, and the study's findings are known only as the Commission reports them. The terms of the closing benchmark are not public, and the EU may return to the chapter (MNE-EU-2026-002-0002). The Government's account of the closure is machine translated and capped at Medium, and gives the venue as Luxembourg in one passage and Brussels in another (MNE-GOV-2026-003-0002; MNE-GOV-2026-003-0004). The Commission does not describe the existing Integrated Health Information System, so how far it falls short of what the card needs is not known.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Montenegro is some months ahead of Moldova on the same route, a feasibility study on public finances followed by an action plan that carries its findings; Moldova finalised its study and approved its EHIC Action Plan in August 2026 (MDA-EU-2026-012-0097; MDA-EU-2026-012-0098). Once those were in place, the Commission's request to Montenegro became concrete: adapt the health information system for the card, equip the insurer and budget for reimbursements by accession. Moldova faces the same tasks with the added one of building an integrated system Montenegro already has. Montenegro had also recognised the card in its health insurance law before the chapter closed, while Moldova plans its law amendments for 2026 (MDA-GOV-2025-002-0072); the case does not show that this recognition, or deferring the card to accession, was what the EU required.
transferable: The sequence of a feasibility study on public finances followed by an action plan with deadlines and responsibilities, which Moldova already mirrors; legal recognition of the card in the health insurance law ahead of its introduction; and the three elements the Commission named for the next step (system adapted for the card, insurer equipped, reimbursement budget), which match the weak administrative capacity and insufficient resources behind Moldova's gap (MNE-EU-2026-003-0005).
not_transferable: Montenegro already has an Integrated Health Information System to adapt, while Moldova has none (MDA-EU-2024-001-0071). Montenegro's study found a basic legal and administrative framework in place (MNE-EU-2026-003-0010), while Moldova states that the EU acts on the card are not transposed (MDA-GOV-2025-002-0063). Montenegro is closing chapters under benchmark terms that are not public, and whether the EU would accept deferring the card to accession for Moldova cannot be judged from the evidence.
notes: RUN-2026-02 comparator step (target Moldova). Comparator case for RUN-2026-02 (Moldova), RI-FMW-015. Closure items MNE-EU-2026-002-0001, MNE-EU-2026-002-0002, MNE-GOV-2026-003-0002 and MNE-GOV-2026-003-0004 are RUN-2026-01 items used as context (chapter-level, no issue assigned); MNE-EU-2026-003-0003 is a chapter-level rating used as context.

description: Serbia is a contrast case: the Commission recorded no developments on the European Health Insurance Card, in identical words, in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, and in 2025 and 2026 asked Serbia in a key recommendation to develop the IT infrastructure for the card. No Serbian measure on the card's domestic preconditions appears in the evidence, and no source says why the position has not moved.
problem_addressed: The 2025 key recommendation asks Serbia to develop IT infrastructures for the EHIC and EESSI, and administrative capacities for the future EESSI network (SRB-EU-2025-001-0013), in nearly the same wording as Moldova's 2025 key recommendation (MDA-EU-2025-001-0021); the 2026 report repeats it (SRB-EU-2026-001-0001). Only the EHIC IT part belongs to this issue, as a matter of administrative capacity. Whether Serbia has a national health insurance card or an integrated health information system is not stated: a search of all 90 Serbian evidence passages in the project for the card, a national health insurance card and a health information system found only the eight Chapter 2 passages of the Commission's 2024 to 2026 reports that mention the card, none of them describing Serbia's systems.
reform_or_mechanism: None in the evidence. Serbia applies agreements on the use of the card with nine Member States (SRB-EU-2024-001-0015; SRB-EU-2025-001-0015; SRB-EU-2026-001-0003), but these concern access through bilateral arrangements, a separate issue outside the scope of this comparison, and are not used in this case.
how_implemented: Nothing to report: the Commission found no developments on the card in each of three reporting periods (SRB-EU-2024-001-0014; SRB-EU-2025-001-0014; SRB-EU-2026-001-0002).
evidence_of_results: None. The unchanged Commission wording across three reports is the only evidence, and it records an absence of change rather than a result.
limitations_of_evidence: Only the Commission's reports cover the card for Serbia: the search of all 90 Serbian evidence passages in the project found no government, research or civil society source on it. The reports give no account of Serbia's systems, plans or reasons, so the case shows that the position stalled, not why.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Serbia received nearly the same recommendation as Moldova in 2025, and the Commission recorded no developments in 2024, 2025 and 2026, including in the year after that recommendation, with no feasibility study or plan visible in the evidence. Moldova has already gone further, with a feasibility study and an EHIC Action Plan in August 2026 (MDA-EU-2026-012-0097; MDA-EU-2026-012-0098), so the contrast mainly shows what the Commission records when such steps are missing. It offers no lesson on the causes of a stall.
transferable: Only as a warning: the Commission recorded no developments in 2024, 2025 and 2026, including in the year after its 2025 key recommendation, so the recommendation alone did not move the position within a year (SRB-EU-2024-001-0014; SRB-EU-2025-001-0013; SRB-EU-2026-001-0002).
not_transferable: Serbia's starting point on the card, its health information systems and its negotiating context on this issue are not in the evidence, so no condition for comparison with Moldova can be stated.
notes: RUN-2026-02 comparator step (target Moldova). Comparator case for RUN-2026-02 (Moldova), RI-FMW-015; contrast case as approved at G1b. No intervention records exist for Serbia on this issue.

description: Montenegro has had an electronic public procurement system under implementation since January 2021. An independent World Bank assessment requested by the country found in 2023 that the system was a good start but needed substantial upgrading and that old technology limited further upgrading, and the EU assigned funds for an upgrade. The Commission reports improvements to the system in each year from 2023 to 2025, but no source in the project shows that the technology limit was removed or that the system was replaced, and there is no measured result.
problem_addressed: The interim findings of the World Bank's MAPS assessment state that the current system is a good start but needs substantial upgrading (MNE-IO-2023-001-0006) and that the assessment found system limitations for further upgrading, namely old technology (MNE-IO-2023-001-0007). This is close to the core of Moldova's issue, an outdated system, but it concerns a system under implementation only since January 2021 (MNE-IO-2023-001-0001). A search of all 204 Montenegrin evidence passages in the project for procurement terms found none that says the system fails to support procedures or stages set out in law, or that it hampers centralised procurement, and none that describes the system used before 2021 or says that the 2021 system replaced it.
reform_or_mechanism: Two linked responses. First, a diagnostic: the Public Procurement Policy Unit asked the World Bank to assess its public procurement system with specific emphasis on electronic procurement (MNE-IO-2023-001-0002), using the MAPS methodology with an e-procurement supplementary module (INT-MNE-0025). Second, an upgrade of the existing system rather than a replacement: the EU agreed to provide further funds to implement the MAPS e-procurement recommendations and assigned funds for the upgrade of the system (MNE-IO-2023-001-0008), and the Commission says the MAPS results will serve as a basis for enhancing the system (MNE-EU-2024-001-0017).
how_implemented: The assessment started in January 2023 (MNE-IO-2023-001-0003), included a dedicated three-day assessment of the e-procurement system (MNE-IO-2023-001-0004), was planned for delivery by January 2024 (MNE-IO-2023-001-0005), and, according to the Commission, ended in December 2023 with a comprehensive evaluation focused on electronic procurement (MNE-EU-2024-001-0016).
