The Commission records some progress in 2023 in improving the functioning of the system (MNE-EU-2024-001-0015), continuous improvements in 2023 to 2024 that facilitate data exchange between institutions and aim at detecting irregularities (MNE-EU-2024-001-0018), and further improvements in 2024 and 2025 to reinforce monitoring and prevent corruption (MNE-EU-2025-001-0020). None of the sources in that search says whether these improvements are the EU-funded upgrade.
evidence_of_results: The only stated effect is the Commission's sentence that improved functionalities of the system facilitate the monitoring of contract award, implementation and appeals (MNE-EU-2024-001-0019). It gives no measure, and it may describe what the system does rather than an outcome. No measured outcome found: a search of all 204 Montenegrin evidence passages in the project for procurement terms found no figure on use, coverage of procedures, processing or monitoring, and no later independent assessment of whether the old-technology limit was overcome.
limitations_of_evidence: The World Bank findings are interim slides by one staff member, stated without the underlying data, and the final MAPS e-procurement report (MNE-IO-2024-002) and the procurement administration's page on the system (MNE-GOV-2025-005) are not available in a usable form, so only the interim slides can be used. In the same search, no passage from the Commission's 2025 report mentions the MAPS assessment or a new system. The Commission's 2025 and 2026 recommendations to introduce a red-flag system, and its 2026 statement that automatic detection of irregularities and the link to the justice database are still awaited (MNE-EU-2025-001-0018; MNE-EU-2026-003-0002; MNE-EU-2026-003-0021), concern a function of a working system, a separate issue, and are context only. The Commission's 2026 report also records a rise in the share of centralised procurement, which it does not link to the electronic system, so it is not used here. No source names the system.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: Moldova is now procuring a new system, with technical specifications received in September 2025 and a call for bids published in December 2025 (MDA-GOV-2026-011-0013; MDA-GOV-2026-011-0016). Montenegro shows that a system introduced in 2021 could be judged within about two years to rest on old technology that limits upgrading, so a new system can itself become the problem Moldova is trying to leave behind. Montenegro's response was an independent diagnostic requested by the procurement policy body, which was then used to secure EU funds for an upgrade; whether the upgrade worked is not known.
transferable: The diagnostic step: an independent assessment of the electronic system under a recognised method, requested by the national policy body, with a dedicated technical review of the system, and its findings used to direct donor or EU funds. Moldova already has funding from international partners and World Bank review of its procurement documents (MDA-EU-2025-001-0063; MDA-GOV-2026-011-0014), and the same mechanism of insufficient resources applies, since both countries rely on external funds.
not_transferable: The response itself: Montenegro upgraded a recently introduced system, while the Commission finds MTender outdated and lacking whole stages of the procurement cycle (MDA-EU-2025-001-0064; MDA-EU-2025-002-0075) and Moldova has chosen to build a new system. The case gives no evidence on replacing a system, on covering every procedure and stage in law, or on centralised procurement, and none on whether the old-technology limit was resolved. Montenegro's procurement policy unit and the body receiving the EU funds are named only by abbreviation, so the institutional set-up cannot be compared with Moldova's.
notes: RUN-2026-02 comparator step (target Moldova). Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-02/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-038.csv; proposed until G6b. Strictness point for the analyst: this case shows a recently introduced system judged technically limited and then improved, not an outdated system being replaced. The red-flag items were moved to RI-TEC-006 at the G5b spot check and are context only. Filing note: MNE-EU-2024-001-0015 is a sub-area rating kept as context, not implementation.

description: North Macedonia runs an integrated electronic public procurement system that the Commission describes as functioning efficiently in every report from 2021 to 2026. The portal was upgraded and adapted to a new legal framework by 2020, modules were added in stages, and an updated version was launched on 1 April 2025, with limited progress recorded on it. No source in the project says the earlier system was outdated, so this is a working system being upgraded, not an outdated one being replaced.
problem_addressed: No source in the project describes the North Macedonian system as outdated or inadequate. The Commission's 2020 recommendation was to upgrade the portal with new modules (MKD-EU-2020-001-0094), and North Macedonia's problem with the system is underuse of modules in a working system, not its age. A search of all 4,629 passages in the North Macedonian evidence files for electronic procurement wording combined with outdated, old, replace, new, re-engineer, updated, upgrade, technology or inadequate found only upgrade and update statements, none stating that the system was outdated or functionally inadequate.
reform_or_mechanism: Incremental upgrading of one integrated system run by the Public Procurement Bureau (INT-MKD-0132; INT-MKD-0133). By North Macedonia's own account in the 2023 screening report, the system covers e-planning, e-publication, e-submission, e-award and e-appeals and its use is obligatory for all contracting authorities and entities at central and local level (MKD-EU-2023-003-0112). The portal was upgraded and adjusted to the new legal framework, with awarded contracts linked to contract notices made available electronically (MKD-EU-2020-001-0095), and the Bureau launched an updated version on 1 April 2025 (MKD-EU-2025-001-0093).
how_implemented: Modules were added in stages: e-appeals became fully operational on 1 April 2019 by the country's account (MKD-EU-2023-003-0115), the e-market for low-value procurement was launched in 2021 by the same account (MKD-EU-2023-003-0113), and the Commission records a red-flag function and a COVID-19 marking function (MKD-EU-2021-001-0050; MKD-EU-2021-001-0053). The system is in use, and the upgrade to the new legal framework has been carried out (MKD-EU-2026-007-0062; MKD-EU-2020-001-0095). The Commission records limited progress with the updated version (MKD-EU-2025-001-0009), and a search of all 4,629 North Macedonian evidence passages for electronic procurement wording found none that states what the 2025 version changed or why it was introduced.
evidence_of_results: The Commission states that the system functions efficiently in 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 (MKD-EU-2021-001-0047; MKD-EU-2022-001-0057; MKD-EU-2023-001-0073; MKD-EU-2024-001-0055; MKD-EU-2025-001-0092), and in 2026 that it operates efficiently, covering all transactions (MKD-EU-2026-007-0062). It credits the electronic procurement and e-appeals system with a high level of transparency (MKD-EU-2023-003-0121); on that statement the system is judged to have worked for transparency, with medium confidence that it contributed. These results concern the system as a whole; no source in the project gives a result for the 2025 updated version.
limitations_of_evidence: The North Macedonian evidence was gathered for the earlier country study and has not been extended, so nothing after the 2026 Commission report is held. The coverage of the cycle and obligatory use rest on the country's own account in the screening report. The listed coverage does not mention contract management. The 2025 update is described in one sentence, and the Commission's limited progress finding gives no detail. Underuse of the e-market and of e-auctions is a separate issue and is not relied on here.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: North Macedonia shows the end state Moldova is aiming for, an integrated system obligatory for all contracting authorities, adapted to the procurement law and judged efficient by the Commission year after year. It does not show how to get there from an outdated system. Once Moldova's new system is working, North Macedonia's staged addition of modules and its single bureau managing the system could guide what follows; Moldova's Reform Agenda pilot already starts with essential modules (MDA-EU-2025-002-0043).
transferable: Adapting the system to the procurement law when the law changes, which answers Moldova's problem of a system that does not allow all tools in the law (MDA-EU-2025-001-0064; MDA-EU-2025-002-0076); adding modules in stages after the core works; obligatory use by all contracting authorities; and one body responsible for the system.
not_transferable: Replacement of an outdated system, which the case does not show. Contract management, which MTender lacks (MDA-EU-2025-002-0075), is not among the stages listed for North Macedonia. The weak administrative capacity behind Moldova's limited progress and its reliance on external funding have no counterpart in the North Macedonian evidence: the same search found no passage linking the procurement system to weak capacity or to donor funding.
notes: RUN-2026-02 comparator step (target Moldova). Seven-part case (E14) in review/RUN-2026-02/run1b/cases/cases_RI-TEC-038.csv; proposed until G6b. Built from validated RUN-2026-01 items and judgements on RI-TEC-006@MKD, reused under E19 with no new collection; North Macedonia's judgements are context, never evidence about Moldova. Strictness point for the analyst: the case does not show an outdated system being replaced, and Low relevance is proposed.

description: North Macedonia's national e-services portal, in use since December 2019, reached 338 services by the end of August 2026, including partly available ones, and the Commission reports that its usage rate doubled from the previous year, after the most-demanded certificates went online in 2025. The rise starts from a low level of use, the rate is not defined, and the Commission links it to the new services only by saying that the two went together.
problem_addressed: North Macedonia's portal was little used: the State Audit Office found 0.556 requests per registered user and that visually impaired persons could not use it (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0194; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0026, machine translated), the Commission recorded 292,179 users but only 2,070 applications a month in 2024 (MKD-EU-2024-001-0024), and 78 institutions still offered 1,120 services only in person (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0055, machine translated). The Commission said in 2024 that the most commonly requested services were not yet online (MKD-EU-2024-001-0021) and in April 2026 still called digital government quite underdeveloped, with most e-services rarely used and only a fraction fully transactional (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007). The audit attributes low use to citizens' weak interest, insufficient promotion and equal prices for electronic and paper documents (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0006, machine translated).
reform_or_mechanism: The portal (uslugi.gov.mk) rests on the 2019 Law on Electronic Management and Electronic Services (INT-MKD-0035) and was upgraded through an EU-funded project to add services, first for businesses and then those most demanded by citizens (INT-MKD-0125; MKD-EU-2025-001-0135). The Reform Agenda sets a payment step to increase the offer of e-services by 50% by June 2027 (INT-MKD-0101; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0091). The long-term ICT strategy SMART/MK plans mandatory integration or connection of each e-service on the portal and a change in the price of e-services (INT-MKD-0489; INT-MKD-0523; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0194; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0197, machine translated), and an analysis for DigInfo centres to support users (INT-MKD-0355; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0127, machine translated). Single Sign-On was integrated across service providers by 2026 (INT-MKD-0317; MKD-EU-2026-007-0098).
how_implemented: Offered: the portal has been in use since December 2019 (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0032, machine translated). Counts differ by source and definition: 392 or 264 at the 2024 baseline, 124 accessible online by September 2024, 314 in the 2025 strategy, and 338 at the end of August 2026 including partly available ones, given as 336 in another chapter of the same report (MKD-EU-2024-008-0013; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0092; MKD-EU-2024-001-0072; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0068; MKD-EU-2026-007-0021; MKD-EU-2026-007-0086). Upgrade: in 2024 the Commission reported only a few new services and the long-awaited 135 not yet configured (MKD-EU-2024-001-0021; MKD-EU-2024-001-0023); in 2025 services for businesses, an easier user interface and new services mostly demanded by citizens, including birth, marriage and citizenship certificates (MKD-EU-2025-001-0135; MKD-EU-2025-001-0136); and in 2026 new services for citizens and businesses (MKD-EU-2026-007-0099). The Reform Agenda step, mandatory integration, the price change and the DigInfo centres remain plans, and progress against the 50% target cannot be fixed because the baselines conflict. Capacity: the audit found 101 of 242 posts for the platform unfilled (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0076, machine translated), and the Commission described ownership as fragmented, with limited resources for the lead ministry (MKD-EU-2023-003-0045).
evidence_of_results: Used: the Commission states that the growth in services 'was accompanied by a growing usage rate, which doubled from the previous year' (MKD-EU-2026-007-0022), and that 2025 and early 2026 saw significant improvements in digitalisation while service delivery still requires efforts to meet EU standards (MKD-EU-2026-007-0019). The starting level was low: about 13 of 100 people aged 18 to 70 were registered on the portal according to the 2025 strategy (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0075, machine translated). A search of all 4,629 passages in the North Macedonian evidence files for usage, user, application, request and end-to-end wording found no count of applications or users after 2024 other than that registration share, which states no reference date, and no share of portal services completed online end to end; the Commission says only that a fraction are fully transactional (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007). Who is served: the Commission says the portal caters for people with special needs (MKD-EU-2024-001-0020; MKD-EU-2026-007-0020), which conflicts with the audit's finding that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0136, machine translated), and in 2026 it finds that digital divides leave rural and older women behind and asks for compliance with accessibility standards (MKD-EU-2026-007-0130; MKD-EU-2026-007-0104).
limitations_of_evidence: The usage rate has no stated definition, base, figure or origin, so the doubling cannot be placed on a scale; the April 2026 statement that most e-services are rarely used describes the level, and the November statement describes the change (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007; MKD-EU-2026-007-0022). The Commission states the link between new services and use only as co-occurrence, and Single Sign-On integration and an easier interface came in the same period (MKD-EU-2026-007-0098; MKD-EU-2025-001-0135). Service counts are not comparable across sources, and the 338 includes partly available services. The audit and strategy figures are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. The North Macedonian evidence was gathered for the earlier country study and its 2026 update; North Macedonia's own assessments are context, not evidence about Moldova. The finding that the upgrade was implemented was made before the 2026 report and has not yet been revisited in its light. Claims of absence in this case rest on searches of all North Macedonian evidence passages in the project, not of the full source texts.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: in North Macedonia, use of the portal rose in the year the services citizens most often request went online, after years in which a growing count of rarely requested services left use low. Moldova's remaining gap sits in a similar place: 61% of citizen services are digitalised against 82% for businesses (MDA-EU-2026-012-0117), and rural demand, which the Commission found low in 2025, rose significantly in 2026, including in rural areas where 118 service centres were set up to respond to persistently low demand (MDA-EU-2025-001-0045; MDA-EU-2026-012-0039). The case suggests ranking further digitalisation by how often citizens request a service, and testing the audit's stated causes of low use, promotion and the price of electronic against paper documents; Moldova's own strategy already proposes lower fees for digital services (MDA-GOV-2023-001-0059).
transferable: As a conditional hypothesis only: putting the most-requested citizen services online end to end and checking use after each addition, promoting the portal, and giving electronic documents a price advantage over paper ones. Moldova already reports the share of services digitalised separately for citizens and businesses, so use could be followed as citizen services are added (MDA-EU-2026-012-0117). The account of causes rests on one audit, machine translated, and the rise in use on one unexplained Commission sentence.
not_transferable: North Macedonia's improvement starts from a narrower range than Moldova's: 338 services including partly available ones, against 636 on EVO of which 447 are online (MDA-EU-2026-012-0038), so the gain from each added service may be smaller in Moldova. Levels of use cannot be compared: a search of all 3,686 Moldovan evidence passages in the project for usage wording found only figures defined differently from North Macedonia's, such as the share of public service users who accessed services electronically (MDA-GOV-2025-003-0173) and active users of the EVO application (MDA-GOV-2026-002-0042). North Macedonia's main constraint is a short-staffed lead ministry, whereas Moldova's government names a cost of digitalisation above its own resources (MDA-GOV-2024-004-0044). Moldova has already set up 118 centres for rural users (MDA-EU-2026-012-0040), where North Macedonia offers only a planned analysis of DigInfo centres, so the case says nothing about assisted access.
